cues.text: Welcome to MIT 8107, Software Development Lifecycle.
This is Study Session 1: Introduction to the SDLC and Planning.
We begin with Chapter 1, what the SDLC is.
The Software Development Life Cycle, or S-D-L-C, is a structured process for planning, analysing, designing, implementing, testing, deploying, operating and improving software.
Notice how wide that list is.
It starts well before anyone writes code and continues long after the software is released.
The purpose of the SDLC is to deliver software that meets genuine needs, and to do so within quality, security, budget, schedule and regulatory constraints.

So success is not just "it runs." It has to be the right software, built to an acceptable standard, kept secure, delivered at an affordable cost and on time, and compliant with the rules that apply to it.
A key point follows from this: coding is only one phase.
Many beginners assume software development means programming.
In the lifecycle view, programming is one stage among several.
Now we need a distinction that students often blur.
A lifecycle model describes the way the phases and feedback are organised.
A methodology supplies practices, roles and techniques.
The model tells you how the phases fit together and how information flows back; the methodology tells you what people do, who does it, and which techniques they use.
The phases themselves may be sequential, overlapping or repeated.
They do not always happen once, in a neat line.
Finally, maintenance and eventual retirement matter as much as launch.
Releasing the software is not the end of the story.
Keeping it running, supporting it, and eventually retiring it responsibly are part of the lifecycle.
Let us now walk through the lifecycle phase by phase.
The table has three columns: the phase, the main activity, and the typical deliverable.
Please look at the accompanying table as we go through it.
The first phase is initiation or planning.
The main activity is to define the problem, objectives, scope, feasibility, risks and resources.
The typical deliverables are a business case, a charter, and an initial plan.
The second phase is requirements analysis.
The main activity is to elicit and validate business, functional and quality needs.
The typical deliverables are an S-R-S or F-R-D, which are a software requirements specification or a functional requirements document, along with a backlog and acceptance criteria.
The third phase is design.
The main activity is to specify the architecture, data, interfaces, user experience and security.
The typical deliverables are a design specification, U-M-L diagrams and E-R-Ds, and prototypes.
U-M-L is the Unified Modeling Language, and E-R-D stands for entity relationship diagram.
The fourth phase is development.
The main activity is to implement, review and integrate code.
The typical deliverables are versioned code, builds, and unit tests.
The fifth phase is testing.
The main activity is to verify requirements and validate real needs.
Keep both words in mind: verifying checks the software against the requirements, while validating checks it against what people really need.
The typical deliverables are test evidence, defects, and an acceptance decision.
The sixth phase is deployment.
The main activity is to release safely into the target environment.
The typical deliverables are a release plan, and a migration plan or runbook.
The seventh phase is maintenance.
The main activity is to monitor, patch, support and improve.
The typical deliverables are incident records, updates, and change requests.
The eighth and last phase is retirement.
The main activity is to migrate, archive or delete, and to decommission.
The typical deliverables are an exit plan and verified disposal.
Verified disposal means you do not merely say the data is gone; you check that it is.
Reading down the table, you can see a pattern: each phase has a purpose, and each leaves behind evidence that the next phase can build on.
Let us return to the first phase, planning, and look more closely at feasibility.
Planning feasibility includes several kinds.
Technical feasibility asks: can it be built?
Economic feasibility asks: is it worth the cost?
Operational feasibility asks: can people use and support it?
Then there is legal or regulatory feasibility, and schedule feasibility.
These are often grouped under the acronym TELOS.
Next, three terms that are easy to confuse.
Constraints are limits.
Assumptions are propositions that require validation, which means you must not treat them as facts until they are checked.
Risks are uncertain events with impact, meaning something that might happen and would matter if it did.
Then scope.
Scope defines what is included and what is excluded.
Scope creep is uncontrolled expansion of that scope.
This leads to a point about change.
Change control is not opposition to change.
Its job is to evaluate the impact of a proposed change and to authorise a revised plan.
So a change is not refused by default; it is assessed, and if it is accepted, the plan is formally updated to reflect it.
Finally, planning also means that you estimate work, dependencies and resources, and that you identify stakeholders and governance.
In other words, you work out how much effort is needed, what depends on what, and what resources you need.
You also establish who is affected by or involved in the project, and how decisions will be made and overseen.
